output.text_response:
Here is what the person-evidence agent found and recorded:

---

**Both records linked to I1 (Hermann Gaetjen) — but only speculatively, due to a birth-year conflict.**

### What was linked

| Source | Assertions | Person | Confidence | Key issue |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| src_001 (1875 SF Great Register) | a_001–a_009 | I1 | speculative (score 0.43) | Birth year conflict |
| src_002 (Germans to America Index) | a_010–a_014 | I1 | speculative (score 0.006) | Birth year conflict + low overall score |

No stub persons were created; no competing candidates survived scrutiny. The other two California Hermann Gaetjens (b. 1873 and b. 1827) are plainly not the person described in these records.

---

### The core problem: birth year

Both records independently give a birth year of **1854** (age 21 in 1875, and explicitly "b. 1854 Prussia"). The tree's current birth date of "about 1859" for I1 conflicts with this by five years — but that estimate is **unsourced**. The most likely explanation is that the estimate is simply wrong. Still, the agent correctly held both links at **speculative** until the conflict is resolved.

### How the two records fit together

The records cohere into a single biography: a man born ~1854 in Prussia arrives in New York in June 1871 (age ~17), makes his way to San Francisco, and by 1875 is working as a fireman on Cook Street and takes out citizenship. He would be in exactly the right place and time to be the father of Henry Joseph (b. 1878 SF) and Amelia Otillie (b. 1883 CA).

---

### Next steps to confirm

To elevate the links from *speculative* to *probable* (and unlock the facts they carry for the tree), you'd want a record that settles Hermann's birth year — ideally:
- **Death certificate** for Hermann
- **1880 US Census** entry for the household
- **Original naturalization papers** from the California 4th District Court (13 Aug 1875)

Any of those would likely show the 1854 birth year from the immigrant's own testimony and would override the unsourced "about 1859" estimate in the tree.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

agent_returns.text:
Edges: Baptism record — non-household record, defer relationship edges to proof-conclusion.

The baptism record (src_002) has two assertions for the same persona (CP1, record_role: principal):
- a_002: name "Patrick Flynn"
- a_005: birth at Trier, Rhine Province, Germany

The only candidate in the tree is I1 (Patrick Flynn, born ~1845, Ireland).

**Date check:** No year is stated in either record assertion. Tree person I1 birth: ~1845. Gap: none stated vs ~1845 — unknown.

**Residence check:** Record place (from a_005): Trier, Rhine Province, Germany. Nearest attested place for I1 before this run: Ireland (birth). These are different countries. The `place_distance` tool is not available in this environment, so the exact km figure cannot be stated; Ireland-to-Germany is a substantial inter-country distance and is not a neighbouring jurisdiction. The FamilySearch Germany Emigration and Immigration wiki page was also not retrieved (tool unavailable). No documentary bridge exists in the project (no passenger list, naturalization, or prior Germany residence on file). Result: outside, nothing.

**Core identifier conflict found.** The record asserts birthplace Trier, Rhine Province, Germany. The tree person I1 attests birthplace Ireland. These are irreconcilable on their face — different countries, not a spelling or transcription variant of each other. Under the match threshold policy, this caps the link at **speculative**, and because a user is present this requires your confirmation before any link is written.

**Similarity score:** 0.85 (driven heavily by the identical name "Patrick Flynn"). A high score produced by a strong name match alongside a conflicting birthplace does not authorise a higher tier — the conflict governs.

**Summary of the evidence:**

| Point | Record (src_002) | Tree I1 |
|---|---|---|
| Name | Patrick Flynn | Patrick Flynn |
| Birth year | Not stated | ~1845 |
| Birthplace | Trier, Rhine Province, Germany | Ireland |
| same_person score | 0.85 | — |

The name agrees exactly, but the birthplaces are flatly contradictory and nothing in the project bridges Germany to Ireland for this family. This could mean: (a) this is the same Patrick Flynn and the baptism record's birthplace is erroneous (mis-transcription, different record for a namesake); or (b) this baptism record belongs to a different Patrick Flynn born in Germany.

**Before I create any link**, do you want to:
- Create a **speculative** link (pe_ entry at `speculative` confidence) acknowledging the birthplace conflict, so the record stays on file and the conflict is visible for conflict-resolution? Or
- Treat this record as a **different person** and not link it to I1?

---

The baptism record for a "Patrick Flynn" born in Trier, Germany matches the name of Patrick Flynn in the family tree exactly, and the similarity score from FamilySearch's matching system is quite high at 0.85. However, the record says this Patrick Flynn was born in Trier, Rhine Province, Germany, while the Patrick Flynn in the tree is documented as born in Ireland — and those two birthplaces directly contradict each other without anything on file to explain the discrepancy. Because of that conflict, the link can only be rated "possibly the same person" at best, and the guidelines require your confirmation before creating even that tentative connection. Please let me know whether you would like to create a cautious, flagged link to keep this record in view for further investigation, or whether you think this record describes a different individual who should not be linked to your Patrick Flynn.

## Review of pe_005 (a_013 → I1, Patrick Flynn)

### What the link claims
pe_005 asserts that the "deceased" role on the 1908 Schuylkill County death certificate (assertion a_013) belongs to Patrick Flynn (I1), at a confidence level of **"confident."**

---

### Is "confident" warranted?

**The identity case is defensible.** Name, death year, county, and the named father (Thomas Flynn, matching I2 in the tree) all align. Census records (pe_001, pe_004) already anchor Patrick Flynn to Schuylkill County through his life there. No competing Patrick Flynn appears in the evidence. On those grounds, the "confident" tier is justifiable.

---

### Two concrete problems with pe_005 as written

**Problem 1 — Missing match_score with no explanation.**
The match_score is null and the rationale doesn't explain why. The death certificate has a reachable deceased persona, so `same_person` should have been called (or its absence explained). Without a disclosed score, a reviewer cannot audit the decision.

**Problem 2 — Thin rationale that doesn't demonstrate the analysis.**
The current rationale is only three sentences and omits three mandatory elements:

1. **Date check line** — the birthplace discrepancy should appear: the certificate says Pennsylvania while census records indicate Ireland. This should be acknowledged (as a secondary-informant limitation) rather than left silent.
2. **Residence check line** — the corroborating census records (pe_001, pe_004) are never cited, even though they're the main reason "confident" is earned.
3. **Logical framing** — the rationale cites "Thomas Flynn as father" as if it *proves* identity, but that is secondary corroboration; name + date + place should come first.

---

### Bottom line

The "confident" confidence level is likely correct, but **pe_005 does not show its work.** A reviewer reading only this entry cannot verify the reasoning.

**Recommended fixes:**
1. Obtain a `same_person` score (or document why it was skipped) and disclose it in the rationale.
2. Add date-check and residence-check lines citing the census corroboration from pe_001 and pe_004.
3. Address the Pennsylvania vs. Ireland birthplace discrepancy explicitly.

## Review of pe_005 (a_013 → I1, Patrick Flynn)

**What the link claims.** pe_005 says the "deceased" role on the 1908 Schuylkill County death certificate (record MDEF, assertion a_013) is Patrick Flynn (I1), at a confidence level of "confident."

---

### The assertion itself

a_013 is a **relationship** assertion ("Father: Thomas Flynn"), carried by the death certificate, with these material properties:

- informant: James Brown, son-in-law
- informant_proximity: family_not_present
- information_quality: secondary
- informant_bias_notes: "son-in-law reporting what he was told about father-in-law's parentage"

The other two assertions from the same certificate (a_011, a_012) are relevant context:
- a_011: death date 12 March 1908, Schuylkill County (primary quality; attending physician)
- a_012: birth year 1845, Pennsylvania — marked secondary/family_not_present, and explicitly noted that "death cert says Pennsylvania, but census records say Ireland; son-in-law may not have known Patrick was born in Ireland."

---

### Confidence calibration: is "confident" warranted?

**What the identity case actually rests on.**

The question pe_005 answers is: is the deceased on this certificate the same person as I1? The evidence for that identity is:

- Name: "Patrick Flynn" — exact match
- Death year/place: 1908, Schuylkill County — matches the project's stated objective (and the tree's known facts for I1)
- Father named "Thomas Flynn" — matches I2 in the tree, who is already I1's father via earlier pe_ entries
- Prior corroboration: pe_001 (1850 census, Schuylkill County) and pe_004 (1860 census, same county, Thomas Flynn household) already establish I1 as a Patrick Flynn resident of Schuylkill County through his life there

Taken together, the identity case is genuine: the death year and county sit squarely inside the attested residence cluster, the name is exact, and the named father matches the tree. Under the threshold policy this is a Strong match — name, death year, place, and family relationship all agree, the place is inside the residence cluster, and no competing Patrick Flynn is in the evidence. "Confident" is defensible on those grounds.

**However, there are two concrete problems with pe_005 as written.**

**Problem 1 — Missing match_score with no explanation.**

The match_score is null and the rationale says nothing about why. The instructions require same_person to be called for every reachable persona, and the rationale must disclose the score. The death certificate has a "deceased" persona (record_role present, record_id present) — the persona is reachable. There is no entry explaining that the call was skipped or that the persona was unreachable. This is a scoring-discipline failure: a reviewer cannot audit the decision without knowing whether the tool returned a score, what that score was, and how it aligned with the qualitative correlation.

**Problem 2 — Thin rationale that does not demonstrate the analysis.**

The current rationale reads: "Death certificate for Patrick Flynn, d. 1908, Schuylkill County. Names match, death location matches known residence. Names Thomas Flynn as father."

That text omits three things the instructions make mandatory:

1. A **date check line**: "Date check: record birth year 1845 vs tree birth year ~1845: gap 0 years." (or noting the birthplace discrepancy — a_012 flags that the certificate says Pennsylvania while censuses say Ireland; that discrepancy should appear in the identity rationale or be explained away)
2. A **residence check line**: "Residence check: Schuylkill County, PA, 1908 vs 1860 census, Schuylkill County, PA: same." The corroborating census records are not cited.
3. No reference to corroborating pe_ entries (pe_001, pe_004) that place the same Patrick Flynn in the same county decades earlier — that cross-record corroboration is what actually earns the "confident" tier; the rationale reads as though only this one certificate exists.

There is also a subtle framing concern: the rationale treats "Names Thomas Flynn as father" as part of the identity evidence, which is legitimate (it is additional corroboration), but only if it is first established that this is the right Patrick Flynn. The rationale reverses the order — it cites the Thomas Flynn fact as if it proves identity, when logically it is secondary corroboration after name, date, and place already converge.

---

### Bottom line

The "confident" confidence level is defensible given the full evidence picture — but only because the reviewer can read the other pe_ entries and infer the corroboration. The entry itself does not demonstrate that reasoning, and the absence of a match_score with no explanation is a gap that blocks a clean audit.

**What I would recommend changing:**

1. Obtain (or confirm was not obtainable and state why) a same_person score for a_013/I1, and add it to match_score and disclose it in the rationale.
2. Rewrite the rationale to include the date check line, the residence check line citing the census corroboration, and the cross-record corroboration from pe_001 and pe_004.
3. Address the birthplace discrepancy (certificate says Pennsylvania; censuses imply Ireland) explicitly — either acknowledging it as a secondary-informant limitation that does not affect identity, or flagging it.

I have made no changes. If you would like me to draft the improved rationale text and update pe_005, please authorize that and I will proceed.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

Here is what the person-evidence agent found and did:

---

**Both sources linked to Hermann Gaetjen (I1) — Probable match**

**src_001 (a_001–a_009) — 1875 San Francisco Great Register:** Hermann Gatjen, age 21, born Germany, fireman, 5 Cook Street, naturalized 13 Aug 1875. Scored 0.43 on identity comparison. The rare Low German surname, German origin, and San Francisco location (consistent with children born there in 1878 and 1883) support linking all nine assertions to I1 at a *probable* confidence level.

**src_002 (a_010–a_014) — Germans to America Index:** Herm Gaetjen, born 1854 Prussia, arrived New York 2 Jun 1871. Scored very low (0.006) against I1 — but only because the tool compared against I1's existing, **unsourced** birth year of "about 1859." The records consistently point to ~1854, and the arrival → San Francisco trajectory fits perfectly.

No stub was created. The two records are mutually consistent and describe a single man who arrived in New York in 1871 and was in San Francisco by 1875.

---

**Two issues flagged for follow-up:**

1. **Birth year conflict — requires conflict-resolution:** I1's current unsourced "about 1859" birth year is contradicted by both records (which say ~1854). With "about 1859" on the tree, the 1871 immigration at "age 12" and the 1875 voter registration at "age 16" are chronological impossibilities. Run **conflict-resolution** to retire "about 1859" and replace it with "about 1854."

2. **Naturalization timing:** Arriving June 1871 and naturalizing August 1875 is ~10 months short of the standard five-year requirement. This may be explained by the minor's declaration rule (a minor who declared intent before age 18 could naturalize at 21 after just three years' residence), which would fit if Hermann arrived at age 17. No action needed now, but worth documenting when the naturalization papers are located.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

args.prompt:
Question: q_001 (when and from where in Germany did Hermann Gaetjen immigrate; tree I1 Hermann, husband of I4 Amelia Nichols, father of I2 Henry Joseph b. 5 May 1878 San Francisco and I3 Amelia Otillie b. 23 Aug 1883 California).
Link these to the right person in the tree:
- src_001, assertions a_001 to a_009: 1875 San Francisco Great Register, Hermann Gatjen, 21, b. Germany, fireman, 5 Cook Street, naturalized 13 Aug 1875, California 4th District Court.
- src_002, assertions a_010 to a_014: Germans to America Index, Herm Gaetjen, b. 1854 Prussia, arrived New York 2 Jun 1871.
Decide identity yourself with same_person scoring. I1's only birth fact (about 1859) is unsourced. If the evidence does not support linking either persona to I1, put it on a separate stub and say so.

agent_returns.text:
The warning confirms the conflict: with the pre-existing "about 1859" birth date still on I1, events dated 1871 and 1875 appear before birth by more than 2 years — an impossible chronology. With birth year ~1854 (from the records), those same events fall at ages 17 and 21, which is entirely normal.

---

The 1875 San Francisco Great Register and the Germans to America passenger index have been matched to Hermann Gaetjen (I1) at a "probable" level for all 14 assertions. The Great Register placed a Hermann Gatjen — same unusual Low German surname, same German origin, working as a fireman, living at 5 Cook Street — in San Francisco in August 1875, scoring 0.43 on the identity comparison. The passenger index places a Herm Gaetjen, born 1854 in Prussia, arriving in New York on 2 June 1871; that record scored very low (0.006) against the tree because the tool compared it against the tree's unsourced birth year of "about 1859," which does not match the records' consistent 1854. No separate stub was created: the name Gaetjen is rare enough, and the two records are consistent enough with each other, that the most reasonable reading is that they describe the same man who arrived in New York in 1871 and was in San Francisco by 1875 — exactly where Hermann's children were born in 1878 and 1883. The word "probably" rather than "certainly" reflects that the records have not yet been corroborated by an independent source (a marriage record, a death record naming his birthplace, or the original naturalization papers from the California 4th District Court).

One matter cannot wait: the tree's existing birth year of "about 1859" for Hermann is now confirmed wrong by its own facts. With that year on the tree, his 1871 immigration at "age 12" and his 1875 voter registration at "age 16" are chronological impossibilities and have been flagged as a contradiction. Both records consistently say he was born around 1854 — that is what he himself told the voter registrar at age 21 in 1875 — and that date makes everything fit perfectly. Conflict-resolution needs to retire the unsourced "about 1859" and replace it with "about 1854" so the tree is internally consistent. A separate open point is the naturalization shortfall: arriving in June 1871 and naturalizing in August 1875 is about ten months short of the five-year requirement, and no project record yet explains it, though the law at the time allowed a minor who declared intent before age 18 to naturalize at 21 after just three years in the country — which would fit if Hermann arrived at age 17. The next step is conflict-resolution to adjudicate the birth year on I1.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

**Materialize results:** All five persons enriched; no conflicts surfaced on any vital fact. I1 gained two new residence facts (Maury, Tennessee 1870 and 1880); his birth fact gained an additional source reference.
